title: How to get an acapella from any song
excerpt: Extracting a clean isolated vocal for remixing, sampling or transcription — which songs give up their vocals easily, how to clean what you get, and where the legal line sits.

body.text: An acapella is the vocal on its own, with the band removed. Producers have wanted them for as long as remixing has existed, and for most of that time getting one meant either being sent it by the label or hunting for a twelve-inch that happened to have an acapella on the B-side. Neither route was available to most people.

Source separation changed that completely. This article covers how to get the cleanest acapella a given record will give up, how to tidy what comes out, and the things worth knowing before you build something on top of it.
The basic process
It is short, and the choices are more consequential than the number of steps suggests.

items: Open the Vocal Remover and load the song.
Choose High quality. For an acapella specifically this matters more than it does for an instrumental, for reasons covered below.
Export as WAV if the vocal is going into a DAW. There is no sense compressing something you are about to process further.
Download the vocal track. The instrumental comes out of the same run — keep it, it is often useful for reference even if you did not come for it.

body.text: If you want the vocal alongside separate drums and bass rather than one combined instrumental, use the Stem Splitter instead. Same engine, more outputs.
Why High quality matters more here

When you extract an instrumental, any imperfection lands underneath a full band and is largely masked. When you extract a vocal, the result is exposed — one voice, alone, with nothing to hide behind. Every artefact is audible.

The six-source model resolves overlapping material more accurately, which shows up as fewer of the two problems that plague acapellas: instrumental bleed underneath the voice, and the watery, phasing quality that appears on sustained notes when a model has had to guess.
The extra wait is worth it every time on a vocal. It is optional on an instrumental.
Which songs give up their vocals cleanly
This varies far more than people expect, and it is worth auditioning a few candidates rather than committing to one.

Best case: a single lead vocal, recorded close, sitting clearly on top of the mix, with moderate reverb. Solo pop and soul records from roughly the last thirty years are frequently near-perfect. Rap and spoken-word deliveries separate exceptionally well, because consonants and rhythmic speech look very unlike any instrument.

Harder: heavy reverb and long delays. The tail of a reverberant word is the voice, spread out and diffused until it looks more like an ambient pad than like singing. Expect a vocal that sounds slightly dry compared with the record, because some of its own reverb has been left behind in the instrumental.

Harder still: stacked harmonies and doubled leads. Four takes panned across the field are four sources, and the model may keep some and lose others, producing a lead that thins out exactly where the arrangement thickened.

Hardest: distorted or screamed vocals, where distortion has added harmonics that make a voice look like a guitar; and live recordings, where the vocal is present in every drum microphone on stage and cannot be fully removed from any of them.
Cleaning up what you get
A raw separated vocal is usually usable straight away, but three cheap moves make a large difference.
Cut the silence

Between phrases, a separated vocal often has faint burbling — the model's uncertainty about whether some low-level residue was voice. Cutting those gaps out entirely with the Audio Cutter removes it completely, and silence between vocal phrases is what you want in a remix anyway.
This one step improves more acapellas than anything else on this list.
Take out the bleed you can hear

If a hi-hat has survived into the vocal, the Noise Remover on a light setting can reduce it, though be careful: it removes constant background, and a hi-hat is rhythmic rather than constant. Keep the strength low and check that the voice has not gone thin.
Trim the top and tail
Cut the file down to where the singing actually starts and ends. It makes the file smaller, it makes it easier to line up in a project, and it removes any intro or outro residue in one move.
Using it in a remix
Three practical notes that save time later.

First, find the tempo and key of the original before you build anything. The bass stem from the Stem Splitter is the fastest way to work out the harmony, because the bass note usually tells you the chord.

Second, if your new track is at a different tempo, time-stretch the vocal rather than the other way round. Modern stretching handles a solo voice extremely well — much better than it handles a full mix — because there is only one source to keep coherent.

Third, a separated vocal is often drier than the original, because some of its reverb stayed behind. That is an opportunity rather than a problem: add your own reverb and it will sit in your track rather than carrying the ambience of somebody else's.
Using it for transcription
The less glamorous use, and possibly the most valuable.

A lyric that has been mumbled or buried for years is usually obvious the moment the band is gone. So is a melody you have been guessing at, and so is exactly where a singer breathes and how they place a phrase behind the beat.

For anyone learning to sing, an isolated vocal from a singer you admire is a better study aid than any amount of listening to the finished record, because the details you want to hear are no longer competing with a drum kit.
The legal position, briefly
This section matters more for acapellas than for instrumentals, because the intended use is usually publication rather than private practice.

A commercial recording carries two separate rights: the composition — the song itself — and the master recording of that particular performance. An extracted acapella contains the master recording. Building a new track under it creates a derivative work that uses somebody else's master.

Practically: private use, study, and transcription are ordinarily fine. Uploading a remix to a streaming platform without clearance frequently results in it being taken down or monetised on the rights-holder's behalf, which is the system working as designed rather than an injustice. Some artists release official acapellas precisely so that people can remix them legally, and remix competitions exist for the same reason — those are worth seeking out.
This is not legal advice, and rules vary by country and by platform. The point is simply that separation being easy does not make publication permitted.
Common problems
The vocal sounds thin
Usually reverb that stayed with the instrumental. Add a little of your own; it will sound more natural than the original's would have in a new context anyway.
Harmonies are missing or wobbly
Stacked vocals separating unevenly. Try the six-source model if you have not. Beyond that, this is a limit of the material rather than the tool.
You can hear the instrumental underneath
Check your source file first — a low-bitrate MP3 is the usual culprit. Then try High quality. Then cut the gaps, which removes most of what you notice.
Sustained notes warble

The signature of a model resolving a passage where voice and instrument occupy the same space. It is worst on long held notes over sustained chords. Sometimes a different section of the same song is clean and can be used instead.
Judging a separated vocal properly
Solo it in headphones and every acapella sounds flawed. That is the wrong test, and using it will make you discard usable material.
The right test depends on what you are going to do with it.

items: For a remix: play it over the track you intend to build. Artefacts that are glaring in isolation frequently disappear the moment there is anything underneath.
For a sample: audition only the phrase you plan to use, looped. A vocal can be perfect for four bars and rough elsewhere, and you only need the four bars.
For transcription: you do not care about artefacts at all, only intelligibility. A rough vocal is fine.
For release as an acapella: this is the only case where soloing it in headphones is the right test, because that is how it will be heard.

body.text: Being clear about which of these you are doing saves a great deal of unnecessary reprocessing.
Getting the timing information you need
An acapella without tempo and key information is much harder to use than it needs to be, and both are quick to establish.

items: Tempo: run the original through the Stem Splitter and use the drum stem. Counting a bare drum track is far easier than counting a full mix, and most software will detect it automatically from percussion alone.
Key: use the bass stem. The bass note is usually the root of the chord, so the first and last bass notes of a section tell you most of what you need.
Downbeat: mark where bar one actually begins. An acapella that starts mid-phrase will not line up in a project, and finding the true downbeat later is fiddly.

body.text: Write all three into the filename. Six months from now the file will be useless without them.
Handling the awkward cases
The vocal has a long delay throw
Producers frequently throw a long echo on the last word of a phrase. Separation usually keeps the first repeat and loses the tail, so you get a vocal with a delay that stops abruptly.

Two options: cut the delayed repeats out entirely, leaving a dry vocal you can treat yourself, or keep them and add your own delay so the tail continues naturally. The second sounds better when it works.
Backing vocals appear and vanish

Stacked harmonies separate unevenly, so a section can thin out exactly where the arrangement was thickest. If you only need the lead, cutting the harmonies out deliberately is more consistent than leaving them to flicker.
The vocal is doubled with an octave

Common in pop and in electronic music. Separation may keep one octave and lose the other, which changes the character noticeably. Try the six-source model; beyond that, this is a limit of the material.
There is a talkbox or vocoder

Neither is really a voice from the model's point of view — both are an instrument being shaped by a voice — so they may end up in the instrumental. If that is what you came for, expect to work harder for it.
What to do with a vocal you extracted
Beyond the obvious remix use, three things are worth knowing.

Chop it. A vocal cut into individual words and syllables becomes an instrument you can play, which is the basis of a great deal of electronic production. Use the Audio Cutter to mark every phrase and export them together in one pass.

Time-stretch it rather than the backing. A solo voice stretches far more cleanly than a full mix, because there is only one source to keep coherent. If your track is at a different tempo, move the vocal.
Pitch it into your key. Within a few semitones a voice shifts convincingly. Beyond that the formants move enough that it reads as a different singer — which is occasionally exactly what you want.
Keeping the instrumental too
The run that produces your acapella produces the instrumental as well, at no extra cost. Keep it even when it is not what you came for.

It is the fastest reference you have for the original arrangement while you build something new, it tells you what the vocal was sitting against harmonically, and it is what you will want the day you decide to make a karaoke version of the same song. Deleting it means running the separation again.
The short version

items: Use the best source file you can find; it sets the ceiling.
Always choose High quality for a vocal — the result is exposed, so artefacts show.
Cut the silence between phrases. It is the single most effective cleanup step.
Expect a drier vocal than the record, and add your own space.
Private use is fine; publishing a remix needs clearance.
